stories.headline: OIL CRASHES 4.49% ON U.S.-IRAN DE-ESCALATION HOPES, SPLITTING STOCKS
stories.body: WTI crude tumbled 4.49% to roughly $96 a barrel after reports that Washington and Tehran are nearing a framework to ease tensions, lifting energy-cost-sensitive cyclicals even as the S&P 500 slipped 0.52% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 fell a sharper 1.39%. The divergence shows traders rotating out of richly valued AI-infrastructure names into the sectors that benefit most directly from cheaper crude.
stories.explain: Lower oil prices cut input costs for airlines, transports, and industrials while easing the inflation pipeline that feeds into Fed policy, so cyclical and value-tilted stocks typically catch a bid on days like this even when the broad tape is mixed. Mega-cap tech, by contrast, trades more on long-duration earnings assumptions and crowded positioning than on the price of a barrel of crude, so it sold off anyway as some of the year's most popular AI trades got trimmed.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD EASES TO 4.89% AS TRADERS LEAN INTO A DECEMBER FED CUT
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield slipped 3 basis points to 4.89%, continuing its retreat from last month's highs, as markets priced a growing chance the Fed trims rates again at its Dec. 9 meeting. The move came ahead of next week's CPI print (Tuesday, Nov. 10), the last major inflation read before that decision.
stories.explain: Yields fall when bond prices rise, and prices rise when investors expect either slower growth or lower future short-term rates — both of which got a boost today from the prospect of cheaper oil feeding through into softer inflation data. A lower 10-year also lowers the discount rate used to value long-duration assets like growth stocks, which is why today's yield move and the Nasdaq's underperformance look contradictory at first glance but actually reflect two different forces — rate expectations versus a crowded-trade unwind — pulling on the same market at once.

stories.headline: GOLD CLIMBS TO $3,957 EVEN AS THE GEOPOLITICAL RISK IT USUALLY TRACKS FADES
stories.body: Spot gold rose 1.19% to roughly $3,957 an ounce, extending its 2026 rally even on a day when easing Iran tensions would normally argue for less safe-haven demand. The move points to a separate driver: falling real yields and continued central-bank buying, not war risk, are what's underpinning gold right now.
stories.explain: Gold pays no yield, so its opportunity cost falls — making it relatively more attractive — whenever real interest rates (nominal yields minus inflation expectations) decline, which is consistent with today's drop in the 10-year. Central banks, particularly in emerging markets, have also been steady buyers for several years as a hedge against dollar-reserve concentration, a structural bid that can keep gold rising even when the day's newsflow would otherwise argue for a pullback.

stories.headline: DOLLAR SLIPS TO 101.78 AS RATE-CUT BETS BUILD
stories.body: The ICE U.S. Dollar Index eased 0.12% to 101.78, tracking the pullback in Treasury yields as traders add to bets on a December Fed cut. A softer dollar is a modest tailwind for dollar-priced commodities, including today's gold rally.
stories.explain: The dollar's value against other major currencies is closely tied to the interest-rate differential between the U.S. and its trading partners — when U.S. rate-cut expectations rise relative to, say, the eurozone or Japan, the yield advantage of holding dollars narrows and the currency tends to soften. That's a direct, mechanical link back to the 10-year yield move in today's brief, and it's also why dollar direction is one of the more reliable day-to-day predictors of gold's dollar-denominated price.

stories.headline: DIVISION I SEASON TIPS OFF MONDAY WITH NO. 1 FLORIDA HOSTING MIAMI, REIGNING CHAMP MICHIGAN ON THE ROAD
stories.body: Preseason No. 1 Florida opens its title defense bid Monday at 6 p.m. ET against Miami in Tampa, while reigning national champion Michigan — unranked inside the top 15 after Dusty May left for SMU — tips off on the road. Washington's own opener comes the same night against Colgate at Alaska Airlines Arena, and the Champions Classic doubleheader (Duke-Michigan State, Kansas-Kentucky) follows Nov. 10 in Chicago.

stories.headline: WEMBANYAMA POURS IN 43 AS SPURS ROUT TIMBERWOLVES FOR FOURTH STRAIGHT WIN
stories.body: San Antonio's Victor Wembanyama scored 43 points with six blocks and seven rebounds in a 121-111 win over Minnesota, extending the Spurs' winning streak to four games and keeping him squarely in the early MVP conversation. Elsewhere Sunday, Memphis improved to a league-best 6-0 with a 136-105 rout of Sacramento.

stories.headline: GIANTS LAND J.J. McCARTHY IN TRADE WITH VIKINGS AFTER DART'S SEASON-ENDING KNEE INJURY
stories.body: New York acquired quarterback J.J. McCarthy from Minnesota for a 2027 fifth-round pick, filling the void left by Jaxson Dart's season-ending knee surgery, in one of several deals completed ahead of the Nov. 10, 4 p.m. ET trade deadline. Dallas also landed cornerback Joey Porter Jr. from Pittsburgh, and Baltimore added center Cam Jurgens from Philadelphia, as contenders reposition before the clock runs out.

stories.headline: UNRANKED USC STUNS NO. 2 OHIO STATE 30-18 AS TRUE FRESHMAN FAHEY'S DEBUT FALLS SHORT
stories.body: True freshman Luke Fahey went 21-of-38 for 260 yards and a touchdown to Jeremiah Smith in his first career start, but Ohio State settled for four field goals and a 2-of-10 red-zone clip in the 30-18 loss at the Coliseum — the week's biggest upset. The result drops the Buckeyes outside the top 10 ahead of Tuesday's first College Football Playoff rankings, the same weekend No. 1 Miami and No. 5 Notre Dame set up a top-five showdown for Week 10.

sports.detail: Chris Lawson's 25-yard go-ahead touchdown catch with 1:30 left and Alex McLaughlin's 48-yard pick-six off Anthony Colandrea's third interception sealed it; both teams finish 5-3 (2-3 Big Ten). Next: Saturday vs. Penn State at Husky Stadium.

Danny Sprinkle's Year 3 roster, with nine newcomers filling out all 15 scholarship spots, tips off the regular season tonight at Alaska Airlines Arena chasing the program's first NCAA tournament bid since 2019.

deepDive.title: Duration Risk: Why Falling Yields Didn't Save the Nasdaq Today
content: Today's tape looks contradictory at first glance — the 10-year Treasury yield fell to 4.89%, oil crashed nearly 4.5% on Iran de-escalation hopes, and by the textbook, both of those should be unambiguously good for the Nasdaq 100's long-duration growth stocks. Instead, the Nasdaq fell 1.39%, underperforming a modestly weaker S&P 500. Understanding why requires separating two things that get conflated in everyday market commentary: the mechanical effect of a lower discount rate on a stock's valuation, and the behavioral effect of crowded positioning unwinding when a popular trade stops working. Today was mostly the second one overriding the first.

In theory, a stock's value is the present value of all its future cash flows, discounted back at a rate tied to prevailing interest rates. A company whose biggest profits are expected five-plus years out — think AI infrastructure spending — has 'long duration': its valuation is unusually sensitive to that discount rate, the same way a 30-year bond's price swings more than a 2-year note's for an identical change in yields. When the 10-year drops 3 basis points, the math says those far-out cash flows are worth slightly more today, which is why falling yields are normally a tailwind for growth stocks. That relationship held for most of the AI rally over 2024 and 2025.

What the pure duration math misses is positioning. When a trade is as crowded as mega-cap AI has been, with enormous dollar amounts concentrated in a handful of names, any catalyst that makes investors reassess the pace of earnings catching up to that capital spending can trigger outsized selling regardless of what's happening to yields that same day. The clearest precedent is the 'Magnificent Seven' wobble of mid-2024, when several of those same stocks fell on softer-than-hoped earnings even as rate-cut expectations were building — duration said buy, crowding said sell, and crowding won for several sessions before the two forces realigned.

That tension is exactly what to watch heading into next week's catalysts. If falling yields and a softer dollar start pulling capital back into long-duration names once the current round of position-trimming exhausts itself, the Nasdaq could outperform again regardless of what the Nov. 10 CPI report shows. But if CPI comes in hot enough to push the 10-year back above 5% and revive a 'higher for longer' narrative, duration and crowding would both point the same direction — down — and today's modest 1.39% dip could look tame by comparison. The rule for an economics student: don't read one session's cross-asset moves as proof a relationship has broken; wait to see which force is driving the next one.
